transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Dubois, thank you for meeting with me. I know this has been a very long and stressful day for you and your family.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It has been an exhausting day. My daughter is very anxious.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that. I want to start by saying I am very sorry. There was a mistake in how we monitored your grandchild's heart rate today, and I am taking full responsibility for that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What are you talking about? The other doctor told me everything was stable. He said the baby was fine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you were told that, and that makes this even more difficult. The truth is that the heart rate tracing showed some drops, called decelerations, and it was categorised incorrectly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Catégorisé? What does that even mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means we labeled the heart rate pattern as normal when it was actually showing signs of distress. We didn't catch the severity of it for two hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two hours? You are telling me that for two hours you didn't know the baby was in danger?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. It was an error in judgment during the review of the monitor. I apologize deeply for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I felt so relieved when the first doctor spoke to me. Now you tell me he was wrong. Or perhaps you are the one who is wrong. This is... c'est inadmissible. This is unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is. It is completely unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I trusted your team. My daughter trusted you. And you just... you just missed it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I did. I let this happen. I am not going to make any excuses for that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want your apologies. I want to know why the first doctor lied to me. Did he lie?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: He didn't lie intentionally, but he gave you information based on an incorrect reading. He believed the situation was stable because that is how it was recorded.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you are all just guessing?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, we have the data, but the interpretation of that data was wrong for those two hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like a fool for believing the first report. I felt... I felt a certain peace, and now you take it away.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can only imagine how jarring it is to have the floor pulled out from under you like that. It's a terrible feeling to be given a false sense of security.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My daughter is in the other room. How do I tell her that you people failed her son?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be the one to tell her. I will explain exactly what happened so you don't have to carry that burden alone.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now? Is the baby safe?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right now, the baby is stable, but we are changing the management plan immediately. First, I have ordered a continuous fetal scalp electrode monitor, which provides a much more accurate reading than the external one we were using. That is being placed right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Every single tracing will now be double-signed by both myself and the attending consultant every thirty minutes. No one person will be the sole judge of the heart rate.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if it happens again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have also alerted the nursing lead to prioritize this room for immediate intervention if any further decelerations appear. You and your daughter have a role here too. If you notice any change in the baby's movement or if you feel something is wrong, I want you to press the call button immediately. We will treat any concern you have as a priority.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know that this will not happen to someone else.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am documenting this as a formal clinical incident today. We are holding a morbidity and mortality meeting on Tuesday to review exactly why this miscategorization happened so we can change the protocol for the whole ward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tuesday. That is a long time from now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is. But the immediate safety steps—the scalp electrode and the double-signing—are happening this second.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am still very angry.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. You have every right to be. I will stay here with you as long as you need.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to express anger and frustration without interrupting and remains regulated under significant pushback.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and in lay language, but the resident never performed a comprehension check to ensure the patient understood.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, takes full personal responsibility ('I let this happen'), and maintains accountability despite the patient's anger.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('jarring', 'false sense of security') and engages with the patient's emotional bids regarding his daughter.

T.justification: Resident provides specific steps (scalp electrode, double-signing), timelines (every 30 mins, Tuesday), a patient role (press call button), and prevention (M&M meeting).
